In this exercise you won't draw a chart from scratch. Instead, you'll **choose a story** and then **stack ready-made layers** in Miro to build the chart that tells it. Every choice is a design decision, and you should be ready to explain why you made it.

There's more than one right answer, and a few wrong ones.

## How it works

1. **Pick a story.** Read the data below with your partner and finish this sentence: *"The story I want to tell is…"*
2. **Build it.** In the [Miro board](https://bit.ly/dlf-vis-it-exercise){target="_blank" rel="noopener"}, stack one layer for each design decision on your build frame.
3. **Justify it.** Add a sticky note next to your chart explaining *why* you chose each layer.
4. **Review.** Swap with another pair and evaluate their chart using the [checklist](handout.qmd#a-quick-checklist). Find at least one strength and one thing to fix.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Building tips
- **Choose your measure first.** The chart layers are grouped by measure: pick from the dollars drawer *or* the percent drawer, so your data matches your axis.
- **Chart type and color come as one layer.** Find the row for your chart type and the column for your color.
- **Line up each layer.** Every layer is 1600 × 1000. Set its width and height to match, and give it the same X/Y position as your build frame.
:::

## The data

U.S. public library spending on collections, by material type, for fiscal years 2015–2024. These are national totals for all public library systems in the 50 states and DC.

- **Print materials:** books, serials and other print items.
- **E-materials:** e-books, e-audio, e-video, databases and other electronic content.
- **Other materials:** physical formats that aren't print, such as DVDs, audio CDs and microform.

| Fiscal year | Print (\$M) | Print (%) | E-materials (\$M) | E-materials (%) | Other (\$M) | Other (%) | Total (\$M) |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 2015 | 756 | 57.6 | 301 | 23.0 | 255 | 19.4 | 1,312 |
| 2016 | 756 | 56.1 | 342 | 25.3 | 250 | 18.6 | 1,348 |
| 2017 | 754 | 54.8 | 374 | 27.2 | 248 | 18.0 | 1,376 |
| 2018 | 755 | 53.3 | 419 | 29.6 | 243 | 17.1 | 1,417 |
| 2019 | 761 | 52.6 | 449 | 31.0 | 236 | 16.3 | 1,447 |
| 2020 | 658 | 47.3 | 544 | 39.1 | 189 | 13.6 | 1,390 |
| 2021 | 666 | 46.3 | 595 | 41.4 | 177 | 12.3 | 1,437 |
| 2022 | 718 | 47.3 | 619 | 40.8 | 180 | 11.8 | 1,517 |

**Source:** Institute of Museum and Library Services, [Public Libraries Survey](https://www.imls.gov/research-evaluation/surveys/public-libraries-survey-pls){target="_blank" rel="noopener"}, FY2015–FY2024 (public domain). Amounts are in current dollars, not adjusted for inflation.

## Questions to discuss

- Does your **measure** match your story? When does a percent tell a different story than a dollar amount?
- Does your **chart type** fit what you want to show: a part-to-whole, or a change over time?
- Does every use of **color** have a reason? Would your chart work for a colorblind reader, or in grayscale?
- Can a reader understand your chart **without looking back and forth** to a legend?
- Can someone state your main takeaway in **5 seconds** from the title?
- Is your chart **honest**? Think about what "current dollars" means over ten years.

See the [companion guide](handout.qmd) for the practices behind each decision.
